transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronan.
Days after congressional Republicans
sustained big defeats in the midterm elections,
President Trump is replacing the White House
Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller.
Miller is the Deputy Chief of Staff
and architect of many of the President's
most controversial policies,
including stepped-up immigration enforcement efforts.
As he departed the White House,
the President spoke with reporters.
- Stephen Miller will be the new Chief of Staff
and Susie's gonna go over to the political operation.
- What do you want, Stephen Miller?
- Just run things well.
- Democrats in Congress are reacting to the news.
Minorly leader Hakeem Jeffries,
who is expected to be the next speaker in the House,
said, quote, "Miller has blood on his hands
"and his presence in government
"should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.
"Fire him now," unquote.
Democrats are preparing to take control
of both houses of Congress in January.
NPR's Frank Langford reports some political scientists
also see significance in the response
to the midterm results.
They're calling it a win for democracy.
- In a survey ahead of the midterms,
most political scientists thought
it was more likely than not
that at least five of the most prominent Republicans
would allege fraud.
That didn't happen.
And President Trump has said he'll accept the results,
which were overwhelming.
Dartmouth Professor Brendan Nihan
is co-director of the survey, Bright Line Watch.
- It's a remarkable turning point.
The threat to democracy has been acute.
It wasn't clear whether he'd be able
to subvert this election, but the system held.
- The White House said Trump was not a threat
to democracy, but a defender.
In a statement, it said,
"President Trump has done more than any other president
"to ensure we have free and fair elections."
Frank Langford, NPR News, Washington.
- Employers in the United States
added 165,000 jobs in October,
far what analysts were expecting.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports.
- A new report from the Labor Department
shows significantly stronger job growth
than forecasters had expected for October.
Job gains for August and September were also revised up.
Industries adding jobs last month include health care,
transportation, and professional services.
Restaurants cut workers in October,
as did construction companies.
The unemployment rate inched down to 4.1%,
even as hundreds of thousands of new people
joined the workforce.
The stronger job market also shows up
in bigger wage gains.
Average wages in October were up 3.1% from a year ago.
That's a bigger annual increase than the previous month,
but still probably not enough
to keep pace with rising prices.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
- Wall Street closed the week with a mixed market
after Thursday's big tech sector sell-off.
The Dow was down, the NASDAQ was positive,
the S&P was also up, ending the week at 7,376.
It's NPR.
Five retired Major League Baseball umpires
are suing the National and American Leagues
in federal court in New York.
They're claiming that baseball underpaid them
more than $2 million in pension benefits.
The five umpires, all of whom served as crew chiefs,
have more than 170 years of service
and officiated more than 21,000 games.
In a 44-page lawsuit, the umpires said
since they worked past the age of 65
and each had 25 years of service,
baseball miscalculated their retirement amounts.
John J. Rockefeller, who served as West Virginia's governor
and a longtime senator, has died.
Chris Schulz reports.
Rockefeller's 50-year career
at every level of public service began in 1964
as a 27-year-old volunteer in the small community of Emmons.
He made a name for himself in Charleston
and especially on Capitol Hill as an early proponent
of reforming and expanding healthcare for all Americans.
For a 2015 documentary on his life,
Rockefeller told West Virginia Public Broadcasting
his early experiences in the state
shaped that lifetime commitment.
I wanted to be good at healthcare.
It's my general thought if you don't have healthcare,
you don't have anything,
no matter what else you might think you have.
And it was certainly true in Emmons, West Virginia.
Rockefeller is being remembered for his service
to the people of West Virginia,
especially coal miners, veterans, and children.
For NPR News, I'm Chris Schulz in Morgantown, West Virginia.
George's governor has declared a state of emergency
after heavy flooding along the Toccoa River.
I'm Dan Roman, NPR News, Washington.
This message comes from U.S. Bank.
Chief Product Officer, Shruti Patel,
shares why U.S. Bank Business Essentials
is designed to bring together
the key products small business owners need.
Some of our small business owners were telling us
how complicated it was,
having checking in one place, built by in another.
And so our goal was to help business owners
bring it all together by building business essentials.
This was really to help business owners
focus more on growing their business.
Learn more at usbank.com/business.
Member FDIC.

topics.text: President Trump replaces Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller; Democrats react
Political scientists say Republicans' failure to allege midterm fraud marks win for democracy
US employers add 165,000 jobs in October, beating expectations; unemployment at 4.1%
Wall Street closes week mixed after tech sell-off; S&P 500 ends at 7,376
Five retired MLB umpires sue leagues in New York federal court over $2 million in pensions
Former West Virginia governor and senator John D. Rockefeller IV dies
Georgia governor declares state of emergency after heavy flooding along the Toccoa River
